💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is.
  • Industry observers note that I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment.
  • Sources indicate that "The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This review contains discussions of addiction.

Recent findings suggest that I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is. Let's use the original run of "Gossip Girl" as an example. This delightfully dishy show started out as a series about teenagers behaving badly in Latest York City and became a flat-out soap opera — in the best way — where characters marry princes, make deals with God after near-fatal car accidents, and sell each other for hotels. My point is that "Gossip Girl" made a choice, at a certain point, to steer into the proverbial skid and just be as absurd and insane as possible, because the show knew it was high camp, not high art.

Industry observers note that I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment. Created by Rebecca Cutter and adapted from May Cobb's book of the same name, "The Hunting Wives" premiered in the summer of 2025 and introduced Netflix audiences to Brittany Snow's Sophie O'Neil, who moves from Cambridge, Massachusetts to the heartland of Texas when her husband Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) gets a lucrative job working for oil tycoon and political hopeful Jed Banks (Dermot Mulroney). When Sophie — who's in recovery as an alcoholic after killing a pedestrian while intoxicated behind the wheel back in Cambridge — encounters Jed's wife Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman), she finds herself drawn into Margo's social circle and drawn to Margo herself, and the two start a torrid affair as teenagers start turning up dead in the seemingly idyllic community of Maple Brook.

Sources indicate that "The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever. If you liked how hot and nuts the first season was, you'll be happy to hear Cutter has turned the dial up to 11.

Sources indicate that after the Season 1 cliffhanger ending where Sophie accidentally kills Margo's beloved but law-breaking brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), there's a lot to deal with in Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives." Jed is continuing his run for governor, but both he and Graham are furious that their wives cuckolded them; Sophie and Margo are estranged over the fact that Sophie figures out, in the final episode, that Margo is responsible for the death of the teenaged Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe). (Margo isn't one of 2025's best TV villains for nothin'.) Despite this, the two end up in bed together pretty promptly in Season 2, and they're just as hot together as ever; if you loved all of the steamy scenes in "The Hunting Wives" Season 1, rest assured that there's plenty for you to enjoy here.

According to recent reports, across the board, Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" takes everything you loved about Season 1 and delivers it in spades. Guns are blazing, kisses are passionate and steamy, and the interpersonal drama is as wild as ever; Brittany Snow and Malin Åkerman are excellent, once again, as two women locked in a love affair that constantly threatens to derail both of their lives. Even as the stakes get sillier and higher, Snow and Åkerman treat every moment that they're on-screen, separately or together, with the utmost seriousness. Remember what Michael Caine did in "A Muppet Christmas Carol?" That's basically what these two powerhouses actresses are doing in "The Hunting Wives," but with considerably more nudity ... and it rocks. The second outing of "The Hunting Wives" forces Margo and Sophie the most heightened situations imaginable, but thanks to Snow and Åkerman's performances, you believe that they're hopelessly in love.

My biggest critique of a show as fundamentally unserious as "The Hunting Wives" is that its lack of gravity can brush up against legitimately serious in-universe challenges. By that, I mean Sophie's drinking. Sophie killed someone in a drunk driving accident before this show's story began, and even though the show does make you root for her relationship with Margo, it also seems to want to make a larger point that Sophie is addicted to Margo ... especially because Margo typically pours Sophie a drink when they're together. To call this message muddled would be ... generous.

With all that stated, I would certainly hope that people dealing with addiction aren't looking to a show like "The Hunting Wives" for a realistic portrayal of that concern. This is also a show where, by the end of Season 2, the body count is in the double digits — and I actually mean that in two senses, because there's a litany of dead bodies and a ton of newly introduced romantic trysts by the time the season finale's credits roll.

In a recent development, honestly, across the last few episodes of Season 2 — critics received the entire eight-episode season — the number of corpses that pile up gets so out of control that the deaths stopped being shocking and started feeling routine. (Without getting into major spoilers, Brad breaks bad in a big way, and it honestly grows tiresome pretty promptly.) I still want to be clear, though: "The Hunting Wives" isn't prestige television, and it knows it. It doesn't always need to be impeccable or even make sense. It's fun, and it fulfills that qualification pretty beautifully.

Sources indicate that dale Dickey, who's finally getting more recognition after years as a supporting small-screen player thanks to her outstanding supporting turn in the perfect 2026 comedy "Widow's Bay," is a perfect new addition to Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" as Zelda Moffitt, the formidable head of a Texan motorcycle gang who has a connection to Margo's past. Soap opera star Kim Matula is excellent as Nadia Kelly, a reality TV producer with an ulterior motive, and John Stamos and Cam Gigandet have small but impactful roles as talent scout Chase Brylan and Zelda's son "Gentle John" Moffitt, respectively.

According to recent reports, as much as he made my skin crawl, though, I have to give full credit to "The Wilds" alum Alex Fitzalan, who appears as the conniving campaign manager Lincoln Trout. As Jed's upcoming right-hand man — with an emphasis on the word right — Fitzalan's Lincoln is disgusting, reprehensible, and compulsively watchable. I suspect he'll play a pretty large role in Season 3, and as horrifying as he is writ large, I sort of can't wait to see more.

Speaking of Season 3, the sophomore season of "The Hunting Wives" leaves us with such a good cliffhanger — which did genuinely surprise me after the back half of the season got just a tiny bit bogged down with murder after murder after murder — that I cannot wait until the planned third season is available to watch. "The Hunting Wives" is one of the most patently ridiculous demonstrates airing right now, and that's not a bad thing at all; in fact, it's exactly what makes it such an incredibly fun ride from start to finish.

"The Hunting Wives" is streaming on Netflix now.

Industry observers note that SNL surprised fans earlier this season with a David S Pumpkins sketch to celebrate the off-beat spooky character’s tenth anniversary. Current cast member Mikey Day was joined by his OG co-stars Tom Hanks and Bobby Moynihan for what hilariously turned out to be several minutes of freezing in place while James Austin Johnson paused the sketch for his President Trump impression. The bit went over very well with fans at home, but it turns out the broadcast version contained a key change suggested by Tom Hanks who was looking out for everyone’s bodies.

Sources indicate that during the original version, Hanks, Moynihan and Day all apparently froze in really exaggerated and over the top poses. Unfortunately for them, they didn’t realize that Johnson’s part with Trump was going to go on for so long. He ultimately talked for four minutes, which left the Pumpkins trio gassed by the time they had to unfreeze and act again. So, Hanks suggested they make a change before the live show.

Here’s how Moynihan described the conversation he had with Hanks after dress rehearsal to Mashable….

According to recent reports, in between dress and air, Tom came over to me and was like, ‘Hey, so, we’re all going to close our mouths.’ We were all doing our poses for dress, and on air, we’re just (standing there with our arms folded). We knew we had to stand there for the whole sketch. Tom Hanks is a good actor. He knew (we should) keep our mouths shut, keep our arms down. You don’t want to hold them up for the whole seven minutes of the cold open.

Moynihan said they probably would have figured all of this out before dress rehearsal, but they actually weren't paying much attention to the larger sketch. Instead, they spent like an hour talking about how absolutely absurd they felt being back in the costumes David S Pumpkins and the Skeletons, who have their own wild names. None of them ever thought the original sketch was going to hit, let alone lead to a TV special and an anniversary sketch a decade later.

You can watch the sketch in its entirety below….

Sources indicate that that’s the power of SNL though. Some of the sketches that go viral and live on in people’s memories involve sharp political commentary or really thoughtful parodies of society. Others just involve a goofy character or characters that connect with people for whatever reason. David S Pumpkins and the Skeletons are definitely examples of those characters. They’re just so over the top and ridiculous that you can’t look away, even if they’re frozen in the background of a President Trump sketch and trying to stay as still as possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're not familiar with "Casablanca," I have to assume that you're from some sort of alien planet, have been in a coma for decades, or are a newborn baby.
  • That's when Ingrid Bergman's Ilsa Lund walks into Rick's particular gin joint, to sloppily paraphrase one of his best quotes (and we'll circle back to that).
  • Sources indicate that "Casablanca" is, admittedly, stacked from top to bottom with memorable quotes (more on that shortly), but "Here's looking at you, kid" feels like it transcends the very film it came from.

Recent findings suggest that if you're not familiar with "Casablanca," I have to assume that you're from some sort of alien planet, have been in a coma for decades, or are a newborn baby. Directed by Michael Curtiz and written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein, and Howard Koch (whose script adapts the play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison), "Casablanca" centers around the taciturn bar owner Rick Blaine (the incomparable Humphrey Bogart), an American ex-pat living in the titular city in Morocco (which was still a colony of France at the time, as the film is set in December 1941). As Rick accepts refugees and ex-pats of all stripes (and has an anti-Axis and anti-Nazi past of his own), he also quietly ensures paperwork to people looking to escape the Nazi regime.

That's when Ingrid Bergman's Ilsa Lund walks into Rick's particular gin joint, to sloppily paraphrase one of his best quotes (and we'll circle back to that). After Ilsa and Rick had a beautiful love affair in occupied Paris and planned to escape together, Ilsa simply vanished, which gave us the bitter, cynical, and lovelorn Rick we see living in Casablanca. Not only is Ilsa back, but she needs a favor: Her husband Victor Laszlo (Paul Henreid), whom she believed was dead when she romanced Rick in Paris, needs papers to evade the Nazis hunting him so that the couple can run away to Portugal (which is unoccupied). Not only does Rick give Ilsa the papers that she and Victor need, he gives up the woman he loves so that she and Victor can live their lives safely. "Casablanca" is a sweeping story of righteous protest against fascism, lost love, and sacrifice ... and "Here's looking at you, kid" is one of its most memorable lines.

Sources indicate that "Casablanca" is, admittedly, stacked from top to bottom with memorable quotes (more on that shortly), but "Here's looking at you, kid" feels like it transcends the very film it came from. There are probably people out there who don't even know that this sweet nothing came from this 1942 classic (and I'd like anyone who doesn't to sit their butt down and watch all of "Casablanca" right now), yet the fact of the matter is that "Here's looking at you, kid" has stood the test of time and remains one of the most immortal lines in movie history.

Industry observers note that so, why is that? Rick says this line to Ilsa throughout "Casablanca," and we see him utter it during flashbacks to the couple's happier times in Paris and right before he puts her on the plane with Victor that will take her to Portugal safely. It's simple but unbelievably meaningful. Before understanding why Ilsa suddenly left Paris, Rick was furious that she vanished from his life. When she reveals that she only left because Victor was alive, sick, and needed her help after he escaped from a concentration camp, his heart softens, and he's able to forgive her for the heartbreak she caused. Rick loves Ilsa, and there's no denying that Ilsa loves Rick, but she's in love with Victor — and the film smartly doesn't villainize Victor, making him a genuinely decent guy who simply wants to escape enemy forces and live peacefully with his wife after years of torment. "Here's looking at you, kid" is Rick's expression of love for Ilsa, and him saying it right as he puts her on a plane that will take her away forever is both heartbreaking and romantic.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I vividly remember learning the phrase “uncanny valley” in 2019.
  • Sources indicate that even though I recently got my first dog, I’ve always been a big cat guy.
  • Sources indicate that so for Polygon’s annual Turkey Day celebration, during which we celebrate the “turkeys” that flopped hard but we can’t help but love, I felt obligated to finally watch Cats and write about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I vividly remember learning the phrase “uncanny valley” in 2019. First came the trailer for Sonic the Hedgehog that April, with those alarmingly human teeth. Then came the first trailer for Tom Hooper’s Cats in July. Suddenly, there was a name for a feeling I’d had my whole life. The uncanny valley is that uneasy feeling you get when something looks or moves almost like a real person, but some small detail makes the whole thing feel wrong. That feeling is a lot more common these days, now that AI-generated videos are everywhere. But it was Cats that really brought the uncanny valley into the popular lexicon.

Sources indicate that even though I recently got my first dog, I’ve always been a big cat guy. I’ve had two cats for almost 16 years. I also love musicals and regularly listen to tracks from Hamilton, Rent, and Dear Evan Hansen. Heck, I also consider myself a Swiftie. By all accounts, Cats seems like something I should have become obsessed with years ago.

Sources indicate that so for Polygon’s annual Turkey Day celebration, during which we celebrate the “turkeys” that flopped hard but we can’t help but love, I felt obligated to finally watch Cats and write about it. Was it worth it? I’m still not sure. I can see why Cats earned a measly 19% from critics and 53% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes. The CGI is often distractingly bad, the tonal whiplash is enough to give you a headache, and I’m pretty sure that the story has always been kind of terrible. Despite that, I found the whole thing feverishly fun and, more often than not, surprisingly sexy. (You know, for something with cat people in it.).

Victoria (Francesca Hayward) is a young cat abandoned in a London alley. She’s taken in by a group of felines called the Jellicles on the night of their annual ball, during which Old Deuteronomy (Judi Dench) will choose one of them to ascend to the Heaviside Layer and be reborn. The candidates make their cases by performing songs. If you want to know why there’s a cat named Skimbleshanks and what he does on the railway, boy, does he have a number for you.

There’s a plot in there, especially once Idris Elba, who is genuinely great as Macavity, starts getting rid of the competition with his teleportation powers. (Also, why do some cats have magic powers?) Most of the movie plays like a series of vignettes in which a newly introduced cat reveals up and sings about the one thing it really wants you to know about itself. That makes some sense for a stage musical adapted from a book of T.S. Eliot poems about different cats. Onscreen, it means the movie keeps asking you to get invested in a new character just as you’ve adjusted to looking at the last one. But because each has a distinct musical styling and energy, the whole thing feels rather uneven and muddled as it shifts between mania and despair on a dime.

In Cats, everything rides on how much you enjoy spending a few minutes with each cat. Some are delightful. Some are horrible disasters. Hayward, a Royal Ballet dancer when she’s not covered in fur, is exceptional throughout as the latest cat on a dizzying adventure. Steven McRae as Skimbleshanks is probably the most energetic and entertaining of them all. Rebel Wilson as Jennyanydots and James Corden as Bustopher Jones are both the epitome of cringe and perhaps the best examples of why Cats struggles as a movie.

Industry observers note that I spent an embarrassing amount of time watching Cats thinking about clothes. Corden’s Bustopher Jones looks like he’s dressed for dinner in a sort of half-tuxedo. Most of the cats just have fur, including Wilson’s Jennyanydots. There’s a moment when she sort of falls off a chair in a way that really plays up the buffoonery of fat cats. Then she rolls onto her back and exposes herself to the camera — it makes you want to shriek and cover your eyes — but then her tail appears strategically propped up between her legs. Not long after, she’s singing into a tail when her actual tail is clearly still behind her. Later in the same number, other cats peel off her outer layer of fur to reveal an outfit underneath, with yet another layer of fur. (WTF?) There’s also a point where she starts eating cockroaches that, like all of the cats, are people in animal costumes. (WTF!?).

I’ve never looked at either of my cats and thought, You are naked. But the Jellicles have human faces and mostly human bodies. There are no visible nipples or genitals. Why are some fully clothed? Why are some partially clothed? Does the existence of the clothing make the others seem even more naked than before? Why does there appear to be a correlation between a cat’s age and the amount of clothing they wear? Why didn’t the production design commit fully to one extreme or the other?

One of the funniest things I’ve ever heard was a rumor that, at one point, all of these cats had buttholes. According to an anonymous crew member whose account was reported by Vanity Fair in March 2020, the simulated skin and fur folded in ways that accidentally resembled buttholes and genitals in roughly a dozen unfinished shots. An anonymous visual-effects editor told The Daily Beast that one crew member was literally brought in to remove all of the buttholes. #ReleaseTheButtholeCut.

It has been revealed that jason Derulo’s Rum Tum Tugger was the first cat I was genuinely excited to spend a whole song with. Derulo plays him like a guy who knows everybody in the room is looking at him and would be insulted if they stopped. There’s even a part where Victoria is dancing with her leg stretched up into the air. He leans his face in. For a fleeting moment, you can’t tell if he’s going to use her foot as a microphone or suck on her toes​​​​​​​. For a certain kind of pervert, Cats can get decidedly sexy. It wants your mind to go there on more than one occasion.

When Taylor Swift demonstrates up rather late in the movie as Bombalurina and dumps catnip on a room full of cats, the sexual energy is dizzying. The song itself is mediocre at best, but the vibes are immaculate. There’s something refreshing about a number where the movie seems fully aware of how horny it’s being. For a few minutes, I stopped trying to figure out how anybody’s fur worked and just enjoyed the song. (Is this Taylor Swift’s sexiest music video ever? Probably.).

It has been revealed that the biggest bit of tonal whiplash comes with Jennifer Hudson’s Grizabella. Hudson has an incredible voice (she’s an EGOT winner!​​​​​​​) and really gives it her all for “Memory,” but Grizabella spends every one of her scenes scream-cry-singing about feelings of rejection and lamenting her lost life as a really cool cat. Hudson once told Empire that she had no idea her character would have ears or a tail, and all of the snot pouring out of her face​​​​​​​ is real. It’s powerful stuff, but also dreadfully unappealing. For me, similar numbers work in something like Les Misérables, where​​​​​​​ the narrative builds up to powerful emotional beats. In Cats, it just feels like a total buzzkill. It made me grateful that Old Deuteronomy selected Grizabella as the Jellicle Choice, which itself feels like a bizarre form of ritual sacrifice and rebirth, if only so she would stop.

Seven years after learning the phrase “uncanny valley,” I finally understand why people wanted to watch Cats together and yell at the screen. My wife refused to watch it with me, so every time I wanted to turn to somebody and say, “Did you see that?” I had to sit there alone with whatever I’d just seen. More often than not, I was pleasantly uncomfortable.

According to recent reports, I’ve seen people argue that Cats falls short of “so bad it’s good.” I think it gets there. It helps if you’re willing to embrace the silly fun and admit that people wearing digital fur can be kind of sexy​​​​​​​. Does that make me a furry?

21 Best Thanksgiving Movies to Stream This Week

📅 24 Nov 2021 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course.
  • Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater.
  • This isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly an appetite for Thanksgiving fare in film. Look no further than the inclusion of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Miracle on 34th Street or Wednesday Adams’s sinister (if historically-accurate) re-enactment in Addams Family Values for proof that audiences love turkey’s least favorite holiday. Of course, Thanksgiving tends to get a better treatment on TV, inspiring canonical episodes of Gossip Girl, Friends, Master of None, and, of course, A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater. Here’s to finding post-meal common ground with one of the titles on this list.

This isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing. You know the story: Steve Martin’s uptight marketing executive, Neal, just wants to travel from Upcoming York to Chicago for turkey with his family. His plans for an uneventful trip are foiled again and again by John Candy’s boisterous shower-ring salesman, Del, who’s eager to make friends with Neal during their wayward journey. We will never look at pillows—or rental car agents—the same way again.

Sources indicate that don’t let the word Christmas in the title scare you away. This 2016 ensemble comedy starring Danny Glover, Kimberly Elise, Mo’Nique, and Gabrielle Union has undeniable Thanksgiving vibes. Produced by Will Packer and originally sold to Universal Pictures under the title A Meyers Thanksgiving, Almost Christmas follows the dysfunctional Meyers family as the family patriarch, Walter Meyers (Glover), tries to get through his first holiday season after the death of his wife. While it isn’t exactly about Thanksgiving per se, most of the best moments in Almost Christmas—including Elise chasing Romany Malco away from the table with a shotgun, or the whole table having to pretend to like Mo’Nique’s terrible food—take place during large family gatherings around the dinner table. What could be more Thanksgiving-coded than that? With an all-star cast of Black actors that also includes J.B. Smoove, Nicole Ari Parker, Omar Epps, and Gladys Knight, Almost Christmas feels like a homecoming full of your favorite uncles and aunties. And, to be fair, isn’t Thanksgiving almost Christmas?

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting carved up in this holiday slasher. Starring Patrick Dempsey and Tik Toker turned recording artist turned film actress Addison Rae, Thanksgiving begins with a Black Friday sale gone horribly awry in Plymouth, Massachusetts, leading to the death of multiple customers. The following year, a murderous slasher wearing a John Carver mask is wreaking havoc in Plymouth, and targeting Rae’s Gaby and her friends. If you’re not feeling warm and gooey on over the holiday, you might want to throw on Thanksgiving and watch Rae and Dempsey’s Sheriff Eric Newton try and track down and escape the clutches of a grisly murderer.

In Jodie Foster’s comedy, Holly Hunter plays Claudia Larson, who returns home for Thanksgiving after losing her job and learning that her daughter (My So-Called Life–era Claire Danes) looks to spend the holiday with a boyfriend. The family she returns to is filled with colorful performances from Anne Bancroft and Charles Durning as her eclectic parents, Robert Downey Jr. as her misanthrope brother, and Dylan McDermott as a semi-mysterious dinner guest.

In a recent development, fantastic Mr. Fox isn’t technically about Thanksgiving, or even really about humans. And yet, Wes Anderson’s 2009 stop-motion film, featuring the voices of George Clooney and Meryl Streep, has been labeled a Thanksgiving must-watch. Perhaps that’s because the film, based on Roald Dahl’s classic children’s novel, is all about animals trying to escape the tyranny of farmers—something every turkey not lucky enough to be pardoned by the president wishes it could do around Thanksgiving time. Beyond the war between animals and farmers, Anderson’s rustic color palette filled with burnt orange—and the massive feast that brings a diverse array of animals around a dinner table after they successfully joined forces to steal food from their nemeses—are full of the spirit of Thanksgiving.

Recent findings suggest that at times, the titular April’s (Katie Holmes) fate feels as if it rests on whether she’ll successfully cook a turkey in her crowded Lower East Side apartment. As April prepares to host her suburban Pennsylvania family, the high-stakes nature of spending a day hunkered down with relatives—played by Patricia Clarkson, Oliver Platt, Alison Pill, and John Gallagher Jr.—rushes in.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes getting families together over the holidays is fraught. In this 1997 moody drama directed by Ang Lee, two affluent Connecticut families unravel over Thanksgiving break as their secrets come to lights. The ensemble cast includes stalwart actors Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, Sigourney Weaver as messy parents, and, at that point, up and comers, Tobey Maguire, Elijah Wood, and Christina Ricci as their even more troubled teens. The Ice Storm, which won best screenplay at Cannes Film Festival, is rife with adultery, substance abuse, as well as surprising turns from a host of talented actors and a sharp early film from one of cinema’s most celebrated directors.

Recent findings suggest that nothing feels more nostalgic during Thanksgiving than watching Snoopy whip up a makeshift meal with jelly beans, popcorn, and mountains of buttered toast for all of his Peanuts pals. And Vince Guraldi’s timeless score makes for a perfect soundtrack to your own festivities.

A Thanksgiving flashback provides key context for the complicated dynamics amongst this group of recently-reunited college friends, played by Glenn Close, Kevin Kline, Jeff Goldblum, Mary Kay Place, and William Hurt. Lawrence Kasdan’s film earned three Oscar nominations, including best picture, original screenplay, and supporting actress for Close.

Industry observers note that while not a Thanksgiving-themed film, protagonist Nola Darling (Tracy Camilla Johns) invites all three of her potential suitors to a tense dinner on that very holiday, making her memorable decision between them from her head-of-the-table vantage point. This was most of the world’s introduction to Spike Lee, both as an actor and director, and the electricity is still palpable. And if you’ve gotta have more? You can always stream the 2017 Netflix original series of the same name, starring Lee and DeWanda Wise as Nola Darling.

Sources indicate that rian Johnson’s whodunnit has all the trappings of a Thanksgiving movie, without ever mentioning the holiday. There’s family infighting, Chris Evans in a cable-knit sweater, foggy fall weather, and even a political allegory about the treatment of people of color. Also not about Thanksgiving, but worthy viewing for the full family: Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, which hit theaters last November.

According to recent reports, the same year that Merriam-Webster acknowledged Instagram captions everywhere by adding “Friendsgiving” to the dictionary, a movie of the same name was released. True to its titular tradition, a group of friends convenes for a meal that inevitably devolves into chaos.

In a recent development, while not an outright Thanksgiving movie, 1997’s ensemble dramedy contains some of the most sumptuous shots of food ever committed to film. After the death of their family matriarch, a group of disparate relatives must put aside their differences and reconvene for a weekly Sunday dinner. Starring Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long, Soul Food captures the bonding powers that plates of cornbread, catfish, and collard greens can bring.

It has been revealed that this 1976 best picture Oscar winner stars Sylvester Stallone as the eponymous down-on-his-luck boxer, whose fate begins to change with the meeting of his future wife, Adrian (Talia Shire). “To you, it’s Thanksgiving. To me, it’s Thursday,” Rocky tells Adrian as he whisks her away from a disastrous family feast minutes after her brother Paulie (Burt Young) hurls her turkey into the nearby alley. As fans of the franchise, which has debuted several films over the Thanksgiving holiday, know, their Thanksgiving meet-cute will stand the test of time.

Thanksgiving isn’t always about bickering with your blood relatives. Spend Thanksgiving with Instant Family, which stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as Pete and Ellie Wagner, an unwitting couple who, overnight, become parents to three foster children. Their decision to become parents happens over  a tense Thanksgiving dinner where Ellie’s family shares they don’t think that Pete and Ellie were ever really cut out to be parents. In an effort to prove them wrong, the Wagners wind up biting off more than they bargained for as they become foster parents to three children, the eldest played by Madame Web star Isabela Merced.

Before Greta Gerwig forced Noah Baumbach to write Barbie with her, there was Mistress America. Written by the real-life couple who helmed the billion dollar blockbuster, this 2015 Sundance favorite centers on the unlikely friendship between Lola Kirke’s Tracy, a first-year college student alone in Latest York, and Gerwig’s Brooke, the Times Square-living twentysomething who will soon become her stepsister. Conflict between the pair gets resolved on Thanksgiving at New York City’s Veselka, a Ukrainian institution where pierogis stand in for the traditional bird.

Greta Gerwig must really love Thanksgiving. The auteur’s Oscar-nominated take on the Louisa May Alcott classic is brimming with cozy, Thanksgiving-esque vibes. Set largely in the weeks before Christmas, the March sisters (Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, and Florence Pugh) and matriarch (Laura Dern) battle wits, trot through the snow, and stage living room plays in a film that feels reminiscent of many a-family gatherings.

“First, let’s give thanks to our families not being here. It’s always easier without the family,” Adam Sandler’s George Simmons, a stand-up comedian who has been newly diagnosed with cancer, states to a group of upcoming friends. In Judd Apatow’s 2009 dramedy, George attempts to revamp his fledgling career in the eleventh hour with the help of aspiring comic Ira Wright (Seth Rogen). At one point, he  joins the younger talent’s friendsgiving festivities, where the table is surrounded by stars including Jonah Hill, Jason Schwartzman, Aubrey Plaza, and Bo Burnham.

Industry observers note that in one of the newer entries to the turkey day canon, Stephen Karam adapts his 2015 Pulitzer finalist play of the same name, exploring the long-held resentments and deeply-rooted admiration that live in an East Coast family. Jayne Houdyshell reprises her Tony-winning role as Deirdre alongside a stacked ensemble, including Richard Jenkins, June Squibb, Beanie Feldstein, Steven Yeun, and Amy Schumer, all gathered in a drab Chinatown apartment for Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that prisoners finds Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal teaming up to find a pair of missing girls who were abducted after Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania. EGOT recipient Viola Davis also stars in the thriller as the mother of one of the kidnapped girls. Directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, Prisoners is an unconventional and unsettling Thanksgiving film.

Another unconventional choice, Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man is arguably the only superhero movie that doubles as a Thanksgiving movie. While the central action follows Tobey Maguire’s Peter Parker, there’s a pivotal scene set at Thanksgiving dinner that directly follows a heated battle between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin (a.k.a Norman Osborne, played by Willem Dafoe.) Parker and Osborne have Thanksgiving dinner together with MJ (Kirsten Dunst), Harry Osborne (James Franco), and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris). During the meal, Osborne comes to the stunning realization that Peter Parker is, in fact, Spider-Man. Others have already made the case that the first Spider-Man film deserves to be included in the Thanksgiving canon. The way Dafoe carves the turkey is also both sinister and iconic, as is Maguire apologizing for his tardiness because he “had to beat an old lady with a stick to get these cranberries.”.

Industry observers note that marvel Cinematic Universe fans and viewers interested in general Marvel content outside the shared universe are in luck, as three TV indicates are coming to Disney+ in December with latest episodes, and they are filled with major heroes. December is set to be the most important month of the year for the MCU's slate of projects, and that is saying something.

Sources indicate that after all, Marvel has had many hits in 2026, with MCU TV highlights on Disney+, such as Daredevil: Born Again season 2 and VisionQuest, and the July release of Tom Holland's Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day. That film became the 3rd highest-grossing movie of all time with over $2.5 billion, and on December 4, it will return to theaters, with Spider-Man: Brand New Day's re-release including an Avengers: Doomsday scene.

That said, the Avengers movie is the biggest release the MCU has on the way in the next month, but also of 2026 as a whole. After all, this is the first film for Earth's Mightiest Heroes in the Multiverse Saga, bringing back beloved stars like Chris Evans, as Steve Rogers, and Robert Downey Jr., now as Doctor Doom. Avengers: Doomsday will also finally unite the Avengers, the X-Men, and the Fantastic Four in live-action.

Industry observers note that while all eyes are on the substantial screen, December will also feature three Marvel TV highlights releasing new episodes on Disney+. Two of them feature major heroes, but exist outside the MCU canon, though in a shared universe of their own, while the other is led by an MCU fan-favorite, and it sets up Avengers: Doomsday. These are the Marvel shows being released on Disney+ in December:.

Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends is an animated series for young viewers, helping kids get used to seeing Marvel's superheroes in action. Season 1 will be back with new episodes on the streaming service on December 1, starting the month Downey returns to the MCU with an Iron Man release, which is fitting, even though Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends bears no connection to the MCU.

It has been revealed that the Iron Man animated series features a lot of characters from Marvel Comics, though it focuses on a main trio, including Tony Stark/Iron Man, Riri Williams/Ironheart, and Amadeus Cho/Iron Hulk. Other notable Marvel characters include Vision, Ultron, Black Panther, Hawkeye, Thor, and more.

The Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast is the only MCU-related series on Disney+ next month, with two episodes on the streaming service's schedule, coming back on December 3 and 10. The podcast focuses on a duo of hosts, MCU Ms. Marvel actress Iman Vellani and Frank Alvarez, as they rewatch key movies in the lead-up to Avengers: Doomsday. The Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast's first episode was focused on The Avengers and was released on August 27.

It is informative for those trying to remember key details before the next Avengers movie, get caught up if you missed a project or more, and also get insights from guests like Chris Evans, Robert Downey Jr., and many more. Additionally, Vellani is not only Marvel's Kamala Khan actress, but she is a genuine MCU super fan, making the podcast engaging. Recent episodes explored Deadpool & Wolverine, Shang-Chi and The Legend of The Ten Rings, and Black Panther: Wakanda Forever. December 3's episode will focus on Thunderbolts*.

Industry observers note that finally, the other animated Marvel series on the list is Marvel’s Spidey and his Amazing Friends, which is coming back with a holiday special in its fifth season. The Spider-Man TV show started the shared universe that Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends is a part of, with these versions of Spidey and Iron Man teaming up in multiple Avengers specials.

Recent findings suggest that this is the flagship show of the "MCU for preschoolers" universe. Marvel’s Spidey and his Amazing Friends started the trend of animated demonstrates in the franchise featuring a key trio, with two versions of Spider-Man, aka Peter Parker and Miles Morales/Spin, and Gwen Stacy as Ghost-Spider. Characters like Captain America, the Hulk, Iron Man, Rocket Raccoon, and more also show up. It is the final show on the list of Marvel releases on Disney+ in December 2026.

#131582. Tech Report: The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Doubles Down On A Once Upon A Time In Hollywood Controversy

Tech Report: The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Doubles Down On A Once Upon A Time In Hollywood Controversy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • It has been revealed that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself.
  • That promptly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

It has been revealed that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself. After wowing audiences everywhere in 2019 with "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the quirky and uber-talented filmmaker returned to the scene of the crime (so to speak) once more with his long-awaited sequel/spin-off film, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." This time, the buddy comedy act with Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton and Brad Pitt's Cliff has been dropped, focusing solely on the latter as the stuntman embarks on his latest round of mischief. Though Tarantino stepped aside from his directing duties to make room for David Fincher, well, let's just say that the script is as purely QT as it gets.

That promptly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before. You see, despite so much acclaim from critics and fans alike, "Once Upon a Time" drew the ire of many with its irreverent treatment of martial arts legend Bruce Lee, portrayed by Mike Moh in the film. Even Lee's family weighed in on the matter, objecting to how easily Cliff puts the arrogant Lee in his place during a fight scene on the set of a film. Not surprisingly, "Cliff Booth" returns to this fraught topic on several occasions, and it certainly feels like a meta-textual jab at the real-world backlash from before.

Was this in poor taste, or is Tarantino merely poking fun with a self-deprecating running joke? Moviegoers will undoubtedly have strong takes on either side. Here's where we land on our second go-around with this little debate.

Sources indicate that you know, there's something to be noted for addressing an uncomfortable matter head-on instead of dancing around it — or even ignoring it altogether. Quentin Tarantino has never been one to shy away from a fight, a trait he happens to share with washed-up stuntman Cliff Booth. As a master cinephile, a brilliant bartender, a hit with the ladies, and a ruthless killer all in one, the power fantasy of it all isn't exactly hard to see in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Perhaps that's what made the Bruce Lee moment in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" stand out all the more (a fight that almost ended very differently). It's one thing for Cliff to be the coolest person alive in his world, and quite another for him to intrude rudely upon our own.

According to recent reports, so how does "Cliff Booth" address this elephant in the room? Although the incident is brought up on a number of occasions in passing, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II's buzzy actor Rodrick "Hot Rod" Harrison is positively fixated on it once he meets Cliff — a fact that also seems to catch the eye of talent manager Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). Intriguingly, Cliff himself almost seems embarrassed by the attention, perhaps self-reflexively brushing it off as the brash actions of a young man. Maybe, like Tarantino himself, he's a little older and a little wiser and less apt to repeat the same mistakes.

Less generously, the fact that this fight is emphasized so much in "Cliff Booth" could make the exact opposite point. It's treated almost like a legend or a myth in this world, giving Cliff a dangerous sense of aura and mystique that belies his charming appearance.

Sources indicate that either way, this is just one ingredient tossed into a much larger stew. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may struggle to reach the transcendent heights of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," but isn't that part of its point, too? "What is Cliff Booth without Rick Dalton?" Quentin Tarantino's script seems to be asking. Not dissimilarly, is a Tarantino movie with David Fincher at the wheel really a Tarantino movie anymore? Who can say how much ownership any of us have over our own art — or our lives in general?

Recent findings suggest that perhaps that's why "Cliff Booth" feels so much colder and mean-spirited than its predecessor. Although both films build to violent climaxes, the one in "Hollywood" is shot to be much more over-the-top and darkly funny than the one here. Before, Rick Dalton and Cliff were fighting to preserve a very specific way of life — one that the Manson family threatened to overturn. Here, Cliff very easily could've avoided the bloodshed with killers Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena), but he pursues this anyway out of ... ego? Principle? A sense of right and wrong? Cliff is a man of both simplicity and contradictions, so perhaps it's only fitting that the filmmaking style reflects this through Fincher's very different approach, as well.

Recent findings suggest that that's where the repeated jabs about the Bruce Lee fight come in, as a moment that Cliff has no choice but to own. "Cliff Booth" is a movie about our attempts to define our own stories — whether it be himself, the troublemaking TV star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), or Karen. And maybe Bruce Lee, too.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in limited theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

According to recent reports, at the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In a recent development, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

It has been revealed that of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

In a recent development, and for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

According to recent reports, there are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

Latest Update: 32 Years Later, Disney's Most Notorious Cash-Grab Sequel Is Better Than You Remember

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever since former Disney CEO Bob Chapek released his autobiography last September, a rather unexpected Disney movie has been a topic for discussion: the direct-to-VHS sequel to Aladdin titled The Return of Jafar.
  • While these sequels — especially The Return of Jafar — were highly profitable for Disney, some felt that they cheapened the work of Disney’s theatrical division.
  • Since then, most Disney fans have come to agree that stopping these movies was for the best, but Chapek, who was in charge of that division for Disney, is still bitter about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since former Disney CEO Bob Chapek released his autobiography last September, a rather unexpected Disney movie has been a topic for discussion: the direct-to-VHS sequel to Aladdin titled The Return of Jafar. Released in 1994, The Return of Jafar was the first in a long line of direct-to-VHS (and later direct-to-DVD) sequels to theatrical Disney films. Besides Aladdin, Disney made sequels to The Lion King, The Little Mermaid, Pocahontas, Mulan, and several other then-modern Disney animated features, as well as some much older classics like Cinderella and Bambi. These movies used cheaper animation produced by Disney’s TV division​​​​​​​ and were developed in far less time than Disney spends developing animated feature films​​​​​​​.

While these sequels — especially The Return of Jafar — were highly profitable for Disney, some felt that they cheapened the work of Disney’s theatrical division. Their chief critic was Pixar head John Lasseter, and when Disney acquired Pixar in 2006, Lasseter convinced CEO Bob Iger to shut down the operation.

Since then, most Disney fans have come to agree that stopping these movies was for the best, but Chapek, who was in charge of that division for Disney, is still bitter about it. In a chapter Chapek titled “Jafar Returns, and I Emerge,” he writes: “Why was there such vocal criticism aimed at the movie? Likely because a bunch of upstart TV animators in their twenties had created something that generated five times the profits of a typical theatrical release … It was Bob from Flyover Indiana, educated at a state school, who disrupted the business and kept the studio afloat with an endeavor others had dismissed as creative heresy.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Chapek’s bitterness is palpable, he’s right about the profitability of The Return of Jafar​​​​​​​, which cost just $5 million to produce and raked in more than $300 million. And while I personally agree that these poorly made sequels​​​​​​​ cheapened the integrity of the originals, I do have a soft spot specifically for The Return of Jafar — but not because it made so much money.

It has been revealed that I was seven years old when Aladdin came out and it quickly became my favorite Disney movie (and it still is). I loved everything about it and even collected the Aladdin action figures by Mattel (including the Genie, which included a cool feature where you could pull out his head and swap his expression with another head stored inside his body). The Return of Jafar came out about 18 months after Aladdin, and I loved the story about Jafar as a genie seeking revenge on Aladdin and the other characters. Sure, Genie seemed a bit different in the sequel (he was played by Homer Simpson voice actor Dan Castellaneta instead of Robin Williams), but he was still my favorite character and still very funny.

Back then, I was too young and dumb to notice the difference between Aladdin and The Return of Jafar from a quality standpoint, but over time — after parting with my Aladdin action figures and gaining a greater appreciation for the process behind Disney's animated films — I grew to understand why Return of Jafar isn’t so good.

However, I’ve since come to fall in love with it all over again for another reason: Gilbert Gottfried.

While Williams didn’t return for The Return of Jafar, the rest of the Aladdin cast did, including comedian Gilbert Gottfried as Iago​​​​​​​, the scheming parrot who sat on Jafar’s shoulders in the first film.

Recent findings suggest that iago was no longer Jafar’s sidekick in the sequel. Instead, he abandons Jafar in the beginning of the movie, as he’s fed up with getting bossed around and hates living inside of a lamp (where Jafar is imprisoned). Iago pulls himself out of the lamp and comes up with a scheme to ingratiate himself with Aladdin, Jasmine, and the others so he can live a cushy life in the palace. And while his strategy is entirely cynical at first, he does find himself caring for the humans he opposed in the first film, especially Aladdin, who seems​​​​​​​ most willing to give him a second chance.

According to recent reports, eventually, Jafar finds a new stooge in the bumbling thief Abis Mal, who finds Jafar’s lamp and begins making hasty wishes. His first wish is for the sunken treasure ship Coeur du Mer, and Jafar teleports him deep into the ocean. Abis Mal then has to use his second wish so he doesn’t drown. As Jafar tells Abis Mal to take some time on his third wish, Jafar plots his takeover of Agrabah and even, temporarily, lures Iago back into his ranks.

In a recent development, as surprising as it might sound, The Return of Jafar is an Iago story first and foremost. He has a more developed character arc than anyone else in the entire movie, and the writers managed to evolve the character without undermining his established self-interest or making him any less funny. He also has two songs that Gottfried scream-sings, and they’re both still hilarious and more catchy than you might think. (“I’m Lookin’ Out for Me”​​​​​​​ is especially great.).

Sources indicate that my renewed affection for The Return of Jafar came about in the late 2010s​​​​​​​ when I began listening to Gilbert Gottfried's Amazing Colossal Podcast, where Gottfried and his co-host Frank Santopadre interviewed showbiz legends every week. Up until that podcast, I had only a vague awareness of Gottfried’s career, mostly as a voice actor, but within a few years he became one of my all-time favorite comedians. As a result, I sought out​​​​​​​ many of his best film and TV roles and, while there were many, Gottfried almost never starred in something. His major personality and raging voice were mostly reserved for small, hilarious cameos. He was never the leading man — except in The Return of Jafar.

(I also encourage everyone to watch the 2017 documentary Gilbert, which is a touching portrait of the man.).

In a recent development, and since Gottfried died in 2022 of Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2, my defense of The Return of Jafar has turned downright personal. Yes, on an objective level, I can recognize the rushed narrative and inferior animation. More broadly, I understand and agree with the idea that Disney’s direct-to-video era hurt Disney’s​​​​​​​ overall artistic legacy, and that The Return of Jafar was the start of all that. But over the past few months, as Disney fans come out against Chapek’s profit-first, art-second defense by bashing this movie all over again, I can't help but think of Iago’s best song lyric from The Return of Jafar, where the aggressive parrot​​​​​​​ shouts, “I'm through with that! I'm flappin' free! From here on in, I'm lookin' out for me!”.

The Return of Jafar is streaming on Disney Plus.

  • 2008's "Tropic Thunder" begins with some table-setting in-universe movie trailers for other fictional films starring the actors who, in the body of the film, are making a Vietnam war movie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, being the third sequel to "Meet the Parents," this week's "Focker In-Law" (you can read our review here) has a lot on its plate. Its intention is to act as a direct follow-up to 2010's "Little Fockers," yet it also aims to lightly reset the franchise's premise and, unlike most other legacy sequels, retain a tight focus on the property's original lead, Greg Focker (Ben Stiller), and his neurotic shenanigans. On the whole, then, writer/director John Hamburg has his hands full with all that plus balancing a rather large ensemble of actors, ranging from returning players like Stiller, Robert De Niro, and Owen Wilson to newcomers such as Ariana Grande. Basically, the film doesn't really have the time to incorporate a bunch of cheeky nods to its stars' past work.

This is why it's even more delightful to see a little tribute to one of Stiller's other popular comedies snuck into the body of "Focker In-Law." Rather than Stiller or the like awkwardly making a verbal reference, the tribute is elegantly woven into a couple of the film's gags. Indeed, one of the tenets of the "Meet the Parents/Fockers" franchise is that Greg needs to be put through the ringer both emotionally and physically, and Hamburg finds multiple ways to accomplish this throughout "Focker In-Law." Near the beginning of the movie, for instance, Greg is accidentally burned in the face, while later, he's nearly frozen to death. In addition to these jokes being part of the movie piling misery onto Greg, they double as a sly nod to Stiller's transgressive action comedy flick "Tropic Thunder," in which his character similarly endured extreme temperatures. It's subtle enough to be missed yet clever enough to stand out.

2008's "Tropic Thunder" begins with some table-setting in-universe movie trailers for other fictional films starring the actors who, in the body of the film, are making a Vietnam war movie. One of these is for a film starring Tugg Speedman (Ben Stiller), and it's the latest in his "Scorcher" franchise. But where the prior "Scorcher" movies have starred Speedman as a hero saving a baby in the middle of a fiery apocalypse, "Scorcher VI: Global Meltdown" sees Speedman's hero return after an eclipse plunges the post-apocalyptic Earth into freezing temperatures. (Also, he's now looking after two babies instead of just one.).

It has been revealed that by comparison, in "Focker In-Law," Greg wants to cook his father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) his favorite meal, but his son's fresh girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande), wants to use the kitchen to make an alternate meal for Jack at the same time. So, Greg and Olivia, having already gotten off on the wrong foot, compete while cooking, which naturally results in Greg becoming careless and nearly burning his own face off, leaving him with a scorched appearance for a while. From there, he goes on to meet up with Jack, who's now all into health and wellness and insists that the pair talk during a cold plunge, which Greg assures him he's done before. But he hasn't, of course, and he ends up not being able to take the extreme cold.

With these two moments combined, Stiller is once again put in the middle of both extreme heat and extreme cold. However, in stark contrast to Tugg Speedman, Greg can't handle either temperature. It's a cute way of acknowledging Stiller's on-screen past while once again dunking pretty mercilessly on Greg.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's no better time to buy a Garmin watch than the Black Friday sales, because it's almost always the period you'll find the lowest prices available on any Garmin.

This year the sale is especially good, because not only have excellent older Garmin watches like the Forerunner 265 and Forerunner 965 returned to their lowest-ever price, but the latest Garmin watches like the Fenix 9 and Forerunner 170 have also been significantly discounted for the first time.

I've been testing Garmin watches for a decade and I think the only watch I can't find a deal on right now is the Enduro 4, but even there you don't have to worry, because the almost equally good Enduro 3 is down to $699 at Amazon.

I’ve picked out 17 deals on the best Garmin watches available right now, from cheaper Forerunner models all the way up to the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, which is $849 in the Amazon sale and still a better buy than the Fenix 9 in the sale, in my opinion.

I think the Forerunner 70 is the best beginner running watch available, and it actually has all the features runners of all levels really need. It's accurate and comfortable to wear 24/7 thanks to its small design, and this is the first time it's dropped under $200 on sale.

The Forerunner 165 is the predecessor to the Forerunner 70 and Forerunner 170 watches, and a good pick, especially for new runners. This is one of the few Garmin deals I'm a little disappointed by this Black Friday, though, because the Forerunner 165 has dropped as low as $129 in the past.

Industry observers note that the Forerunner 170 has a few extra features compared to the Forerunner 70, most notably music storage, and also comes in this delightful teal color ( which I'd say makes it worth the upgrade alone). It's a great running watch and is getting its first big discounts this Black Friday.

This is the biggest percentage discount I've seen on a Garmin watch right now, and it makes the Instinct 3 AMOLED a strong, adventurous alternative to the Fenix and Enduro. It offers incredible battery life and a distinctive, rugged design, as well as reliable sports tracking, but it does lack the maps you get on pricier models.

This is one of the best deals going on for a Garmin right now, because even though the Forerunner 265 is an older watch, it's still an excellent multisport tracker with a bright AMOLED display. It even comes in two sizes and I'd say the only watch that can rival it for this price is the Coros Pace 4.

According to recent reports, the Forerunner 965 is the best alternative to newer top models like the Forerunner 970 and even the Fenix lineup if you're looking for value this Black Friday. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that katrina joined ScreenRant as a news writer in 2024, covering box office, expert interviews, exclusives, and fresh releases. Her work has appeared in CBR, All About Jazz, Rising Artists, and numerous other publications. She has an MFA in Creative Writing and has published more than 20 books. She currently writes for ScreenRant’s movie features team.

Recent findings suggest that steven Spielberg's Catch Me If You Can is available to stream for free, but unfortunately, that will soon change. From Minority Report to Bridge of Spies, some of Steven Spielberg's best crime thrillers blend high-stakes chases with investigation and suspense. While the filmmaker is best known for his work in sci-fi, action/adventure, and historical drama, the thriller genre has a special place in his filmography.

In 1971, Spielberg made his breakout debut with Duel, a television thriller that introduced his feature-length directing career, while Jaws is widely considered his best thriller to date.

Industry observers note that from Harrison Ford to Meryl Streep, Spielberg has worked with some of the best actors in Hollywood over the years, but Tom Hanks has starred in more of the filmmaker's movies than anyone else except Martin Drew. The Forrest Gump actor has appeared in five of Spielberg's feature films. The two have also coproduced three historical miniseries together.

Catch Me If You Can wasn't the first time Hanks and Spielberg worked together, but it's one of the best thrillers the two made together, and it features a rare on-screen collaboration between the Forrest Gump actor and Leonardo DiCaprio.

While Catch Me If You Can is technically a crime thriller about the cat-and-mouse race between FBI agent Carl Hanratty (Hanks) and check forger Frank Abagnale Jr. (DiCaprio), comedy is where it shines the brightest. Spielberg takes a high-stakes concept and makes it heartwarming and humorous.

DiCaprio's Frank is a troubled teenager who struggles after his parents' divorce. Even though the actor has starred in several comedy films, surprisingly, the funny scenes in Catch Me If You Can are almost entirely carried out by Hanks. His FBI agent offers plenty of comic relief. The character is animated at times when he behaves stubbornly and acts adorably clumsy.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI agent falls into Frank's traps just like the con artist's other victims. The scene where Frank slips right under Hanratty's nose is both suspenseful and hilarious.

It has been revealed that diCaprio's con artist is the opposite of Hanks' FBI agent. He doesn't make a fool of himself on screen every few seconds. In fact, Frank is almost too brilliant to get into trouble. Instead of letting himself get bullied on the first day of school, the boy pretends to be the sub teacher for French class and manages not to be caught for a week. By the time his parents are called to the principal's office, Frank is organizing a field trip.

Spielberg always has a sense of humor. Even in a gruesome film like Jurassic Park, the filmmaker makes sure there are scenes (such as the one where a dinosaur attacks a man sitting on the toilet) that offer comic relief, but Catch Me If You Can is where the director's comedy instinct truly shines.

In a recent development, the comedy in the movie is layered. There's humor in the absurdity of Frank's best scams in Catch Me if You Can, as well as Hanks' lack of self-consciousness. However, even with so much comedy in the movie, Spielberg doesn't let it get carried away by these moments.

The intricate balance between crime and comedy is one of the things that make Catch Me If You Can such a brilliant film. Instead of starting in the middle of a high-stakes crime, the movie spends some time with Frank before he runs away from home and starts forging checks. By doing so, it keeps his story grounded in what it's really about: a troubled teen who, in the end, just wants to get his parents back.

In a recent development, spielberg didn't leave any detail untouched. The last scene between Frank and his father tells it all. It turns out all Frank needs to stop running from the government is for his father to ask him, but Frank Sr. insists that running is all his son has left, and because of it, Frank then spends months in Europe, running the same con across countries as Agent Hanratty.

What makes Catch Me If You Can really special is that Spielberg could easily focus on the cat-and-mouse chase between Frank and Agent Hanratty and make it a popcorn thriller, but he intentionally stretched out the story and made the chase only one part of the movie.

From the Christmas phone call ritual that Hanratty and Frank share to Hanratty giving Frank a second chance to work for the FBI, the crime thriller has a lot of heart. It's true that Frank committed fraud and stole millions, and for a while, he was living his life as a criminal, but the movie also indicates the moment the character stops being defined by his past actions, offering hope in the end.

According to recent reports, much of the crime thriller's magic lives in the dynamic between Hanratty and Frank. Without the on-screen chemistry between DiCaprio and Hanks, Catch Me If You Can wouldn't be the same. Frank writes to his father every once in a while to share his "accomplishment," but it's Hanratty who's trying to stop him.

According to recent reports, instead of spending Christmas talking to his family, Hanratty is all Frank had for a long time. Their relationship goes beyond an FBI agent and a criminal. In a way, Hanratty is like a father and a mentor to Frank. He looks out for DiCaprio's character and tries to guide him to use his talent the right way, while Frank's real father encourages him to keep running from the law to justify his own fraudulent past.

Tom Hanks brings out the sturdy and honest side of Agent Hanratty. Instead of lying to Frank to bring him into custody, he really tries his best to save the boy, and that's almost unfamiliar for someone like Frank, whose own parents don't seem to bother to save him.

Spielberg has featured many great lead duos in his movies, but the on-screen bond between Hanks and DiCaprio’s characters is unforgettable.

Catch Me If You Can is officially leaving Tubi's free streaming platform on December 1, 2026. The last day to watch this underrated thriller by Steven Spielberg for free is November 30. While fans with a Paramount+ subscription can still enjoy the movie, it's also scheduled to leave the service on January 1, 2027.

Platforms rarely own a movie permanently. Films like Catch Me If You Can are frequently rotated between services based on the movie's distribution deals across studios and partners. However, it's right now unclear when it'll return to Tubi.
