  • A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset.
  • Sources indicate that given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the newly introduced film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next substantial screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

Sources indicate that given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the newly introduced film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

In a recent development, A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary Fresh Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino mentioned in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”.

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino stated that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report notes that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting newly introduced sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

Recent findings suggest that in a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

It has been revealed that if you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV highlights, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

It has been revealed that “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover fresh sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Calvin and Hobbes contains multitudes as a fantastic comic strip from the 1980s and 1990s, with Bill Watterson's work still celebrated over 30 years since it concluded. It's loaded with approachable philosophical insights and emotional nuance, while told largely through the eyes of a chaotic, complicated young Calvin accompanied by his stuffed tiger, Hobbes. While Calvin has plenty of his own high and low points, though, the sometimes underappreciated aspects of living around or even raising a complex young kid can show itself in occasional instances.

Susie Derkins has certainly been expressive about the difficulties of growing up with Calvin as a classmate and friend, but as for family, it can sometimes show in more bite-sized moments. Calvin's parents, naturally, face each little detail head-on, from general mischief, to house damages, to occasional reminders that, while they invest their lives in raising him, he may amusingly not always realize the work that goes into parenting. But for one November 8, 1993 Calvin and Hobbes strip, Calvin attempts to present himself and his parents' work as a point of pride to his mother, with the comic hilariously cutting to her subsequent reaction.

In a recent development, the scenario is incredibly simple for this two-panel strip: Calvin steps in while his mother works on some household errands at the table, simply saying he's her "massive accomplishment in life!" This is immediately followed by the father arriving home from work to see mom, sunken into the couch, simply remarking, "I'm depressed." It's effective, incredibly concise, and a funny, lighthearted jab at how parents might occasionally feel like everything they sink into raising their kid might not have been enough. Calvin's an expressive, individualistic young kid with a wild imagination and a heart for mayhem with little responsibility, but he's also, crucially, still a kid, which his parents obviously acknowledge.

In a recent development, it's not that Calvin's mom regrets having him, although moments like this are rare blips of regret to which any parent can relate. It's entirely human to have small moments of doubt in oneself as a parent, especially since Calvin's mother is a stay-at-home mom, so any doubts in raising her boy as the "significant accomplishment" of her lifetime are perfectly reasonable. But it's pretty clear from how she's written throughout Calvin and Hobbes that the mother is a proud parent, guilty only of being overwhelmed and exasperated by her son's antics. The best part is, the week surrounding this particular strip alone is loaded with fun moments featuring her.

It has been revealed that in the very next strip released on November 9, 1993, Calvin and Hobbes introduced one such type of incident that would understandably overwhelm all sorts of veteran parents. The strip shows Calvin talking to his mother as she goes through his laundry, having taken in some sort of scary critter, erroneously keeping it in his pockets, and being concerned that she didn't find it, implying it's loose somewhere in the home.

The mom understandably grows concerned by Calvin's carelessness, but never outright takes it out on him. Yet, when unprovoked in other strips in that same week, this same character can happily poke fun at her son when tensions are low, her comedic timing staying on-point while not at any point hurting her child's feelings with her wit.

This is the sign of an effective parent who, while never fully adjusted to the whimsy of raising Calvin, shows enough poise at the right moments with him, while channeling any doubts away from him. Calvin's mom is still prone to completely understandable reactions to her son's most foolish actions. But kids are allowed to be loud, annoying, and irresponsible, while parents are allowed to feel overwhelmed or doubt themselves, on the assumption that it doesn't consume them or harm their bonds with their children.

Recent findings suggest that parents should also be honest with themselves, while being strategic with their hilarious or embarrassing but ultimately harmless truths about their kids, such as confirming that Calvin was, indeed, a very stinky baby. Calvin and Hobbes may largely be about life as a kid, but it also encompasses what goes into raising that kid with love, devotion, and some lighthearted, teasing when the moment calls for it.

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Industry observers note that right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

It has been revealed that the X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

According to recent reports, as much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motivated by the recent breakthrough on the VP vs VNP problem, the consumers (Samuel Everett and Deven Mithal) guided instances of ChatGPT and Claude to develop further, more granular algebraic complexity class separations. This is a work in progress in both the development and dissemination of mathematical research with AI tools, and any feedback is appreciated. The results in this repository grew out of a conversation between Sam and Claude Fable 5.2. The initial prompts were inspired by a separate discussion between Sam and Deven, the latter of whom suggested combining the latest VP-VNP results with some of Sam's private work in the area. Claude Fable 5.2 found the proofs through the conversation with Sam, and then wrote most of the paper under his guidance. That conversation started from initial ideas in a separate, earlier conversation Sam had with ChatGPT Astra 6.2, which proved $\mathrm{BIP}{\mathbb R}^{\times}\subsetneq\mathrm{PAR}{\mathbb R}^{\times}$ (Boolean-message interactive proofs against parallel polynomial time, in the real model with multiplication). The conversation with Claude Fable 5.2 extended that starting point to the further separations listed below. All results are formalized in Lean 4 (see Lean formalization below), with the results cited from the literature as explicit hypotheses. The results have not been peer reviewed and should be read with that in mind.

In the Blum–Shub–Smale (BSS) model, the graph {Y = per_m(X)} of the real permanent lies in parallel polynomial time PAR_ℝ and outside each of.

and over the complex numbers outside NP_ℂ and coNP_ℂ. Each of these classes is therefore strictly contained in PAR_ℝ (respectively PAR_ℂ).

Both closed thresholds, $Y \le \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ and $Y \ge \mathrm{per}_m(X)$, also lie in PAR_ℝ and outside NP_ℝ, coNP_ℝ and Σ₂^ℝ. Negating one matrix row and the claimed value interchanges the thresholds. Their intersection is the graph.

The separations use the superpolynomial lower bound for the border complexity of the permanent (Theorem 2.3 in the paper, cited from the Anthropic manuscript "VP ≠ VNP over every field" and its Lean formalization). Two families of results use no lower bound:.

In a recent development, the directory lean/ contains a formalization of the paper in Lean 4 (v4.36.0) with Mathlib (v4.36.0), about 36 000 lines. To check it:.

Every numbered lemma, proposition, theorem and corollary of §2–§7, Theorems A–F, and Remarks 4.3, 5.4 and 7.4(a) are stated and proved, with no sorry. #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for every result.

The results that the paper cites are explicit hypotheses of the theorems that use them, not axioms:.

In particular, every separation is conditional on PermLowerBound, exactly as in the paper.

Recent findings suggest that fact (S1) holds by construction: semialgebraic sets are defined as first-order definable sets. Baur–Strassen, Ryser's formula, Hoeffding's inequality (from Mathlib) and the unrolling of machines into trees are proved.

Appendix A of the paper (sections/lean.tex) and lean/README.md list the Lean name of each result, the modelling choices, and the few places where a formal proof differs from the text. lean/ClassSeparations/Pinned.lean restates the main statements verbatim and checks them against the proved theorems.

Industry observers note that the proofs have not been peer reviewed. The paper is mostly AI-written (see above). The results are formalized in Lean, conditional on the cited results listed above.

The bibliographic data in refs.bib were checked against publisher and Crossref records. The numbered results cited from the Anthropic manuscript, Bürgisser (2004, 2026), Baartse–Meer, Baur–Strassen and Cucker et al. were confirmed in the sources. Still to be confirmed against the full texts: the attributions to Cucker (1992, 1993), Koiran (1994), Blum–Cucker–Shub–Smale, and the numbering in Basu–Pollack–Roy, which follows the second edition (2006).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee can feel like an overwhelming pastime. There's so much noise online about coffee — grind size, flow rate, milk texture — that I'm surprised any newbies are brave enough to take the plunge and buy their first espresso machine.

It has been revealed that but the most important difference is the type of espresso machine you buy. There are loads of different types of machines for different types of coffee drinkers: superautomatic, semi-automatic, manual, bean-to-cup/all-in-one... the list goes on. Today, let's get to the bottom of it.

Recent findings suggest that what type of espresso machine is best for you, and which should you buy? I'm using Casabrews, Ninja, and De'Longhi espresso machines to exemplify my points today — and they're all on sale for Black Friday.

Sources indicate that the De'Longhi Rivelia is my favorite automatic espresso machine. It has two hoppers so you can switch out beans if you so please, and it makes both hot and cold drinks at the push of a button (but you have to buy the cold frother separately, unfortunately).

The Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best espresso machine under $100 (of the ones I've tested). This machine makes delicious coffee, and while you need to spend a little time learning how to use it, it's totally worth it.

Sources indicate that the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is like the best of all worlds. It has a built-in grinder and tamping assist to prevent messes, and it has both manual and automatic milk frothing. This machine is great for learning how to be a barista.

There's one key difference between automatic and manual machines: ease of use. (Size and price also come into play!).

Automatic machines are called that for a reason: press a button, and you get hot coffee in seconds.

An automatic coffee machine selection screen generally looks something like this.

It has been revealed that some machines have upwards of 50 recipes. The De'Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499) offers 38 recipes — some of which I, an ex-barista, had never heard of — including hot and cold beverages. At the press of a button, the machine makes your drink for you.

Depending on price, some automatic machines have integrated milk frothing, like the pictured De'Longhi Rivelia ($1,499) or the De'Longhi Magnifica Duo ($999).

You don't have to do anything. No grinding, no tamping, no calculating dosage volume. As long as there are beans in the hopper, water in the tank, and electricity in the machine, it'll take care of everything.

Automatic machines are ideal if you drink a lot of coffee, but either you don't have time to make it yourself, or you don't want to make it yourself. Both are valid.

It has been revealed that but what about a manual espresso machine? Manual espresso machines vary in functionality — some have built-in grinders, so closer to automatics, but some are incredibly hands-on. Let's run through a few examples.

In a recent development, this is the Casabrews 3700 Essential. It's the cheapest espresso machine I've rated highly, and my only recommendation for a sub-$100 espresso machine. If you want the cheapest manual espresso machine on the market, I'd go for this one.

Industry observers note that this machine necessitates either a separate grinder or getting your coffee ground for espresso at a local cafe. It comes with dual-walled (pressurized) coffee baskets. While a pressurized basket means it doesn't make "technically" perfect espresso, it's a fantastic machine to learn on, as it's incredibly forgiving.

However, you do need to spend a bit of time learning the ropes. Unlike an automatic machine, you have to do everything yourself. You need to grind the coffee, put the coffee in the portafilter, press "start", and steam your milk.

If you want to get into coffee as a hobby, or you like the routine of making coffee, then I would recommend a manual machine such as this.

However, if you want to make your life easier and you have a little more money to spend, I'd also recommend looking at manual espresso machines with built-in grinders, like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

As you can see, this machine has a lot more going on than the Casabrews 3700 Essential. The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus has a built-in grinder (on the left) and tamping assist (also on the left).

Although you still need to put beans in the hopper and adjust grind size yourself, this machine takes a lot of the hassle out of your morning brew. The Luxe Cafe Mini doesn't have automatic milk frothing, but the Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (pictured) does. The Mini will set you back $449, while the Plus goes for $499. Right now, though, the Mini Plus is $419, and the Mini is $399.

It has been revealed that the long and short of it is this: No time to spend making coffee? Just want coffee, stat? Automatic — De'Longhi Rivelia.

Want to learn the art of coffee, and don't mind buying a grinder or getting your beans ground at a cafe? Manual — Casabrews 3700 Essential.

Industry observers note that still want to make the coffee yourself, but you want a built-in grinder? Manual with a built-in grinder — Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

Recent findings suggest that although not as integral as ease of use, size is also something to consider. In general, automatic machines are pretty huge. Here's a size comparison of our three case studies.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (manual, grinder).

Casabrews 3700 Essential (manual, no grinder).

Sources indicate that if you're short on space, the answer's kind of obvious — it should probably be a manual with no grinder. However, you need to remember you will either require a separate grinder or have to get your beans ground at a cafe.

Obviously, though, automatic machines are much larger than manuals. I would only recommend automatics if you're sure you have the space for them — they look bigger and bulkier than the numbers might suggest.

For everyone in between, I'd go for the Ninja.

Obviously, the more features a machine has, the higher its price. In general, automatic machines will set you back at least $1,000 — the only models I've tested under this are the $999 De'Longhi Magnifica Duo and the $999 Jura ENA4 — the latter of which can't make milk drinks. Honestly, what's the point? If you like black coffee, just get a drip machine like the Moccamaster KBGV Select ($270 right now on Black Friday deal).

After automatic machines come manual machines with built-in grinders. This price can range from $3,000 (Breville Oracle Dual Boiler) to $229 (Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder). As someone who's tested all the cheapest models and all the high-end models, I would be wary of a machine charging less than $400. I'd recommend machines like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini (pictured, $499), Breville Barista Express ($699), and De'Longhi Arte Evo ($699) — the latter of which can make cold(ish) brew!

#131546. Tech Report: How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

Tech Report: How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every visual element in animation helps tell the story.
  • Sources indicate that and by “more,” we mean witches.
  • In a recent development, “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something latest inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

Sources indicate that and by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

In a recent development, “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

Industry observers note that according to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”.

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”.

In a recent development, billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Recent findings suggest that both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”.

Sources indicate that “What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”.

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”.

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie stated yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”.

According to recent reports, bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”.

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush noted. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”.

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush noted.

“Hexed” is now playing in theaters.

Star Wars' Mandalorian-era, lightsaber-filled show returns next year, and it could change everything for the galaxy far, far away. Since its 2019 debut, The Mandalorian has been one of Star Wars' most important stories, not only revitalizing the franchise after the divisive reaction to the sequel trilogy but also exploring a relatively upcoming era of the timeline. Before The Mandalorian, little was known about the New Republic era, despite its crucial placement between the original trilogy and Star Wars: The Force Awakens.

Soon enough, The Mandalorian became more than a show; it became an entire sub-franchise. Alongside the ill-received The Book of Boba Fett, The Mandalorian brought animated Star Wars: The Clone Wars heroes back into the fold, including Mandalorian leader Bo-Katan Kryze and long-lost former Jedi Ahsoka Tano. As Anakin Skywalker's unexpected Padawan, Ahsoka is one of Star Wars' most important characters, a vital player in Anakin's fall to the dark side and the larger Clone Wars conflict.

Ahsoka returned in Star Wars Rebels as an early member of the Rebellion before meeting Din Djarin and the artist formerly known as Baby Yoda in The Mandalorian season 2. Now, Ahsoka has become one of the Fresh Republic era's most influential characters, a genuine threat to the Imperial Remnant. If any character deserves to have a show named after them, it's her.

In a recent development, disney+'s Ahsoka not only continues The Mandalorian's Imperial Remnant storyline but also picks up where Star Wars Rebels left off, with Ahsoka and Ghost Crew member Sabine Wren setting off on a perilous journey to bring back the exiled Jedi Ezra Bridger. Following The Mandalorian and Grogu's less-than-stellar box office run, Ahsoka's second season, set to debut in January 2027, has the power to change the galaxy and the franchise forever, as returned Imperial mastermind Grand Admiral Thrawn wages war against what remains of the Rebel Alliance.

Ahsoka season 2 will determine Star Wars' future on Disney+ and beyond. Though The Mandalorian has largely been a success, The Mandalorian and Grogu's theatrical failure has thrown the New Republic era's storytelling into question. At Star Wars Celebration 2023, Lucasfilm announced Dave Filoni's Mandalorian-era culmination movie, supposedly meant to bring The Mandalorian, The Book of Boba Fett, and Ahsoka together in one last, Avengers-esque Star Wars-themed hurrah, a version of Timothy Zahn's non-canon Star Wars Legends epic, Heir to the Empire.

Given what happened with The Mandalorian and Grogu and all the other theatrical changes since then — Rey's New Jedi Order movie is still in limbo, with next year's Star Wars: Starfighter taking its place as the first post-Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker story — there's a chance this movie will never come to fruition. Ahsoka season 2 could technically conclude Thrawn's story in its eight-episode run (a pivotal battle between Thrawn and Admiral Ackbar has already been confirmed), setting the stage for the First Order's rise to power as seen in the Star Wars sequel trilogy, bringing the so-called "Mandoverse" to an end once and for all.

However, the Imperial Remnant isn't the only threat in Ahsoka season 2. In fact, Ahsoka and Sabine are in a galaxy even further away than Star Wars' primary galaxy, where a powerful darkness lurks in the shadows, waiting to be unleashed. Ahsoka and Sabine will chase Jedi-turned-mercenary Baylan Skoll across Peridea as he hunts the source of this power, potentially encountering the Star Wars Legends-era Force-wielder Abeloth, otherwise known as the Mother.

Industry observers note that given the Mortis gods' statues (the Father, the Son, and the Daughter) on Peridea and Ahsoka's lasting connection to the Daughter after The Clone Wars' Mortis arc, this seems the most likely path. Abeloth is one of the most powerful figures in the Star Wars Legends continuity, a being of chaos and destruction with the power to bring about the end of "everything.".

Covering Thrawn's war against the Rebel Alliance and Abeloth's hypothetical re-emergence in eight episodes will be difficult. It'll need to feel like one cohesive whole, especially since both storylines take place in two distinct galaxies. Introducing a villain like Abeloth — or at least someone or something equally powerful — would need to affect the franchise at large. It can't just be a one-and-done event. That makes it feel more likely that the Mandoverse's arc won't end in Ahsoka season 2, though nothing is confirmed.

Sources indicate that ahsoka season 2 is presently the only live-action Star Wars Disney+ show left; no other projects have been officially announced, with the franchise attempting to return to its theatrical roots. Following the Mandoverse, Lucasfilm may benefit from a more balanced approach, investing wisely in both movies and streaming indicates that not only expand Star Wars' timeline but also its creative scope. For now, though, Ahsoka season 2 essentially holds the keys to the franchise's future.

Ahsoka season 2 premieres on January 20, 2027, exclusively on Disney+.

It has been revealed that lenny Burnham grew up in Missoula, Montana. From an early age, he was obsessed with TV and loved creating websites and participating in fan forums for Buffy the Vampire Slayer. He attended New York University, where he studied Dramatic Writing with a focus in Television Writing.

It has been revealed that he hosts two podcasts about television, House of House: A House Rewatch Podcast and Chapter Surfing, a podcast discussing TV shows adapted from books. He’s previously had freelance articles published in Paste and Inverse. He is a gay trans man who is an expert in looking at television through the lens of LGBT representation. He’s also an avid shipper.

Recent findings suggest that with so many mystery reveals arriving on streaming lately, from Dept. Q to Ludwig, it's getting harder for any one series to stand out. That is part of what makes The Åre Murders feel like such a hidden gem. The smart Swedish crime drama returns to Netflix for Season 2 on December 27. The six-episode season picks up a year later, with detectives Hanna Ahlander and Daniel Lindskog investigating two deaths in Åre just as Christmas approaches. Based on Viveca Sten’s novels Hidden in Snow and Hidden in the Shadows, the five-episode first season follows Hanna (Carla Sehn), a Stockholm detective who gets pulled into the case of a missing girl while visiting the small town of Åre.

Recent findings suggest that in the first episode of The Åre Murders, Harald Halvorsen (Henrik Norlén) and Lena Halvorsen (Sofia Papadimitriou Ledarp) are horrified to realize their teen daughter Amanda Halvorsen (Freddie Mosten-Jacob) has been missing for a full night. Her parents thought Amanda was staying over at a party, but when they checked in with one of her friends, they discovered she had left early, and no one has heard from her since. Hanna joins the initial search for Amanda. At first, she’s not acting in her capacity as a police officer; she’s simply joining a large search party of concerned civilians. But when the search fails, the police open a proper investigation. They’re understaffed and ask Hanna to join the investigation even though she’s on leave. Although Hanna knows she has personal problems to work through, she’s invested in the case and agrees to join.

The specifics of Hanna’s personal problems are slowly revealed over the show’s five episodes, along with the central mystery in which the case of one missing girl leads to larger secrets, including a murder mystery and human trafficking. Carla Sehn’s excellent performance anchors the show as Hanna uncovers multiple brutal crimes. She plays the serious scenes well but also gives Hanna a breezy, flirty quality.

One of the strongest aspects of The Åre Murders is the relationship between Hanna and her newly introduced partner, Detective Daniel Lindskog (The Abyss' Kardo Razzazi). Their partnership starts rocky. When they first meet, Hanna is having a rough moment while driving her brother-in-law’s car. Daniel pulls her over and finds out that not only is she driving a car that isn’t hers, but she doesn’t have her license on her. He only lets her off after finding out she’s a fellow police officer. When she joins the case, he’s reluctant to partner with her. But over the course of the series, they slowly begin to trust each other.

Sources indicate that hanna and Daniel's relationship is sure to please anyone who loves watching crime-fighting partners fall in love. They have strong romantic tension throughout the show. One scene in which Daniel visits her in the hospital is especially sweet and tender. But the best part of their relationship is the less serious moments. In an otherwise bleak show, it's a joy watching how easily they fall into a rhythm of joking around together. At the same time, their dynamic is complicated because of Daniel’s wife and newborn baby.

The structure of The Åre Murders is unusual but intriguing. Partway through the series, it shifts focus to a murder that is seemingly unrelated to Amanda’s disappearance. The disconcerting structure works and creates an engaging two-part mystery. Structurally, the show is similar to Dublin Murders, which adapted two mystery novels into a single season. But The Åre Murders pull this off more smoothly. The Åre Murders works because Hanna and Daniel are such strong characters.

Despite having ‘murders’ in the title, Amanda's case doesn’t actually become a murder case until Episode 2, and it takes even longer for the detectives to start investigating a second murder. The Åre Murders doesn’t have to wear its mysteries on its sleeve because it’s satisfying just watching Hanna try to pick up the pieces of her life and navigate her messy relationship with Daniel. Like Top of the Lake, it’s a character drama first. It's fitting that the end of the series focuses on where Hanna and Daniel are at in their personal and professional lives rather than setting up the mystery for Season 2.

It has been revealed that this focus on character applies not just to the detectives, but also to the friends and family members of the victims. The show holds the audience's attention not with constant wild twists but with how well it dramatizes the distress caused by the absence of the missing and deceased.

The Åre Murders is an intriguing binge, with enough surprises to keep viewers on the edge of their seats until the very end. Like so many other female-led thrillers, its biggest strength is a unique, complex woman at its center, brought to life beautifully by a great actress. Hanna is a flawed and idiosyncratic character who’s always interesting to watch.

The Åre Murders is available to stream on Netflix in the U.S.

#131542. The history of civilization is the history of wheat

The history of civilization is the history of wheat

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Asteriskmag

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, according to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving.
  • In a recent development, together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides.
  • The ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, according to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving. The original gods were forced to live in poverty. To solve this problem they created Ashnan, the goddess of grain, and Lahar, the god of sheep, and sent them to humans to cultivate their gifts.

In a recent development, together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides. But the new gods quarreled about which was greater. Enki, the god of wisdom, judged Ashnan the superior, reasoning that without grain there would be no bread, no beer, and, by extension, no cities and no Sumer.

The ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people. Human consumption of wheat is older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel. In fact, some of the very earliest surviving examples of writing, which, like wheat, originate in the Middle East, aren’t epic poems or religious texts but administrative records of the storage and taxation of grain. Other staple crops dominated in other parts of the world (like rice in East Asia, and maize in the Americas), but it was wheat that fueled the Roman Empire and the Industrial Revolution. Wheat now provides one-fifth of the world’s calories. The fact that it does so is thanks to centuries of human ingenuity and scientific improvement.

Recent findings suggest that six thousand years ago, when the Sumerian civilization was beginning to emerge in what is now Iraq, human consumption of grain was already ancient history. Remains of domesticated wheat from around 10,000 years ago have been found in Anatolia. These leftovers were wild emmer and einkorn (two progenitors of wheat), which looked a lot like the other wild grasses growing around them: a tall stalk topped by a small seed head. They were variably distributed throughout the landscape, and their seeds ripened at different times, so collecting them would have been laborious. Nonetheless, the people of the ancient Levant found the effort worthwhile, as the seeds were calorie-dense and stored well.

Recent findings suggest that by farming wheat, humans unintentionally made it worse but also improved it. Wild wheat had reproduced without human assistance for millions of years. Its seeds, the grains that we eat, are attached to the head of the plant by a thin stalk called a rachis. When the seeds are mature, the rachis shatters, dispersing the seeds on the ground.

Recent findings suggest that this process is essential for wild wheat to reproduce. Human intervention removed this selection pressure, allowing plants that did not shatter to reproduce. Because nonshattering is a recessive trait, nonshattering plants cannot produce shattering offspring.1 As a result, nonshattering plants proliferated, supplanting their wild predecessors. This is how archaeologists observed that domestication was underway.2.

Neolithic farmers collected and planted seeds from the heads of plants that remained intact, whereas seeds that had already fallen to the ground were less likely to be harvested or planted. Stores of emmer and einkorn dated as early as 7600 B.C.E. show rough scars, not the smooth tears left by spontaneous shattering, indicating that the natural reproductive process had been interrupted by harvesters. Once the seed-shattering trait had disappeared, wheat was almost completely dependent on humans collecting and planting its seeds to reproduce. In perhaps a thousand years, millions of years of selection for seed shattering had been undone.

On the positive side, yields went up. Grains grew bigger thanks to human cultivation. Naturally, grain size varied, but larger grains were less likely to be blown away or slip out of harvesters’ baskets and were therefore overrepresented in the seeds saved and replanted. On top of that, humans tend to plant seeds deeper than they naturally scatter, and larger seeds are more likely to germinate at greater depths. These processes are thought to have increased grain size by a quarter over the first 500 to 1,000 years of cultivation. By this time, wheat could no longer thrive without help from humans. But the transition to agrarian, sedentary communities enabled by bigger harvests also marked the beginning of our dependence on farming.

The next important step came just as wheat was beginning to spread to surrounding regions, when it absorbed a whole new set of genes from another species.

According to recent reports, one way plants differ from animals is that they can hybridize much more easily, sometimes even happily adding whole upcoming genomes to their own. Long before domestication, emmer wheat had already done this: Wild emmer is a naturally occurring amalgam of a cousin of einkorn and another species known as goat grass (Aegilops speltoides). Emmer is therefore tetraploid, meaning it has four sets of chromosomes.

Sources indicate that emmer and einkorn wheat diffused throughout Anatolia to Cyprus and beyond as farmers migrated out of the Fertile Crescent. Around this time, emmer hybridized again, incorporating the genome of a second species of goat grass (Aegilops tauschii), bringing its chromosome set count to six. This hybridized wheat, which first appears in the archaeological record in northeastern Turkey around 6000 B.C.E., thrived because it had two valuable traits. First, it was free-threshing. Before this, farmers had to pound grains with a mortar and pestle to free them from their tough outer husks, adding a labor-intensive step to every harvest. Second, this new hybrid had higher gluten content, meaning it could form stronger doughs that hold gas, allowing bread to rise. Initially, this saved labor and enabled tastier food. It is now known as bread wheat, or common wheat, and makes up more than 95% of wheat produced today.

Over the next several millennia, cultivation of bread wheat (and agriculture, more or less) spread throughout Europe and Asia. If a plant failed to grow in its upcoming soil or was killed by autumn frosts before reaching maturity, it would be superseded by its better-acclimated relatives. Over thousands of years, incremental changes resulted in countless subtly different local “landrace” populations. Wheat also evolved through further hybridization with closely related plants. This is how we got spelt, which combined the larger grains of bread wheat with the strong shells of emmer, protecting it against the wet and cold and allowing it to thrive further north.

In a recent development, much of this adaptation was probably incidental, just as early selection for larger seeds and nonbrittle rachises had been. But even in ancient times, careful attention was paid to wheat husbandry and to which varieties thrived in which environments. In 50 B.C.E., the Roman writer Varro advised farmers that “on the threshing-floor the largest and best ears should be placed apart, to furnish the best seed.”3 Long before genetics, farmers understood that good seed begat good crops. This contributed to thousands of years of gradual improvement and specialization.

According to recent reports, the Romans may have been intentionally selecting the best plants, but modern scientific wheat breeding began in western Europe in the 19th century. This dramatically sped up yield improvements. A fortuitously large number of early English estate records have survived, meaning we have data for wheat yields starting from before 1275, at which time farmers were producing around 0.6 metric tons per hectare. This was actually worse than the (continental) Romans, who achieved yields up to 1.3 metric tons per hectare.4 Yields remained approximately flat before the 16th century, when they began increasing (and have not stopped).

From the early 1600s through to 1805, yields in Britain almost doubled, increasing from 0.74 in 1604 to 1.26 metric tons per hectare in 1805.5 Deliberate plant selection contributed to this improvement, but intensive selection — that is, aggressively multiplying the very best strains — didn’t really take off until the second half of the 18th century.

Farmers had always wanted to find high-performing seeds, but now they could buy them. Seedsmen emerged, trading hyperadapted local variants like Red Lammas, a strain popular in the 18th century that was known for thriving in chalky soils and making good-quality flour.

Industry observers note that cereals were significant business: The original London Corn Exchange6 was built in 1747; the Paris exchange in 1767; Amsterdam had its own Korenbeurs more than a century earlier. From 1765, Britons began importing wheat with the express purpose of finding better varieties, and middlemen living in other countries would send samples of promising grains to contacts in Britain. Yields reflect the results of an increasingly commercialized sector. After stasis for hundreds of years, then steady 2.5% per decade growth in the previous two centuries, yields grew 60% between 1805 and 1865.

In the 19th century, progress was still driven by entrepreneurs, usually curious farmers, rather than scientists. One key innovation, pioneered by Patrick Shirreff in Scotland and John Le Couteur in Jersey, was transitioning from selecting a handful of the best plants to breed from, to selecting the best single individual plant, and multiplying it. They didn’t understand the underlying biology, but the results were clear.

In addition to producing more of the best strains, repeated selection and rebreeding of individuals made the traits of the multiplied strains more consistent from generation to generation. As with shattering seed heads 10,000 years earlier, rebreeding meant undesirable genetic variants were eliminated from the population. Early breeders called this “breeding true,” and though the genetic basis for it was not yet understood, it was vital to farmers, who prefer more consistent and predictable crops.

According to recent reports, another important development was the intentional crossing of two plants to create a hybrid. A wheat plant can self-pollinate because it contains both male and female reproductive organs, fertilizing its ovules with its own pollen. The overwhelming majority of wheat plants are produced in this way, and therefore have just one parent, which acts genetically as both mother and father. This process doesn’t produce clones initially because each pollen grain or ovule, even from the same individual, is genetically distinct. But it does result in offspring with extremely limited genetic diversity, which diminishes even further with each successive generation of self-breeding.7.

It has been revealed that but sometimes cross-pollination produces plants that come from two parents rather than one. In nature this occurs randomly, but plant breeders deliberately take pollen from one plant and use it to fertilize the ovule of another. Shirreff was a pioneer of this technique, too. The best offspring resulting from these crosses would outperform both parents on some key traits. These high-performing varieties would then be multiplied and the seed sold to farmers.

These techniques were adopted throughout Europe, where the Vilmorin Seed Company in France and the Swedish Seed Association in Sweden were among the first to institutionalize cereal breeding. In 1884, The Technology of Bread-Making identified as many as 65 wheat varieties, local and imported, available in English grain markets.

Before the Industrial Revolution, Britain was a largely agricultural nation. But by the end of the 19th century, the population had increased more than sevenfold from about 4 million people in 1600 to 30 million in 1900, and only a tenth of workers were employed in agriculture. This would have been impossible without improvements in agricultural yields. The “dark satanic mills” of the Industrial Revolution needed wheat just as much as they needed coal and child labor.

Industry observers note that the pace of improvement increased as researchers began to understand more about genetics and evolution. The discoveries of Darwin (natural selection) and Mendel (the inheritance of simple genetic traits, like seed shattering) were essential to understanding why and how techniques applied over the previous centuries had worked. Also critical were contributions of Wilhelm Johannsen, who untangled how much traits were shaped by genes as opposed to the environment, and Ronald Fisher, the “father of modern statistics,” who figured out the underlying maths. Fisher also showed how continuous traits like height could be determined by the cumulative effect of many individual genes. These insights, around 100 years ago, led to the development and widespread adoption of statistical tools to identify the best seed varieties and to predict how their offspring would perform.

Recent findings suggest that breeders generated a vast array of new varieties for testing through a combination of exploration and crossing. Exploration, which was often sponsored by the state, meant collecting seeds from the many unique wheat varieties that had proliferated across the earth since the dawn of time. Britain’s Watkins Landrace Wheat Collection, for example, created in the 1930s, acquired more than 800 wheat cultivars from 32 countries, which could be crossed to create more than 300,000 new hybrid varieties. The USDA had the largest program. Using genetic material from these collections, nurseries would generate crosses for initial testing, multiplying the seeds until there were enough to carry out trials. Trials across several locations allowed researchers to distinguish the effects of genes and environment.

But there were still constraints holding back wheat yields. One was wheat rust, a fungal disease that leaves a characteristic orange-brown powdery residue on plants before shriveling and killing them. Ancient writers knew about this disease: The Romans even had a yearly festival, the Robigalia, in which they performed rituals meant to keep it at bay. In the worst-affected years of the mid-20th century, wheat rust was killing off nearly 20% of American wheat. Breeding programs developed resistant varieties, but any respite was short-lived as the fungus would rapidly evolve a new line of attack.

Industry observers note that another was wheat plants “lodging,” or falling over under their own weight. Fertilizer had become much cheaper thanks to the Haber-Bosch process for making ammonia from nitrogen gas, developed in 1909. But its usefulness for improving wheat production was limited because although fertilizer could in theory make the plants grow larger than before, applying it would often make the stems collapse, making the wheat unharvestable.

At the time, these problems seemed to show that there were fundamental trade-offs limiting yields. It was assumed that further improvements would be incremental. This fueled worry that there would soon be insufficient food for the growing global population; biologist Paul Ehrlich predicted in 1968 that “in the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death.”.

Recent findings suggest that these gloomy forecasts turned out to be dead wrong. Between 1950 and 1990, wheat yields in many countries — rich and poor — doubled, as did the yields of other crops: the fastest improvement to farming efficiency ever seen. This explosive growth, enabled by advances in breeding together with mechanization and the wider adoption of fertilizer, is referred to as the “Green Revolution.” Norman Borlaug, an American agronomist often called the father of the Green Revolution, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work. In 2009 the director of the World Food Programme stated that Borlaug “saved more lives than any man in human history.”.

According to recent reports, borlaug didn’t discover anything fresh — he just implemented existing techniques better than anyone had before. In 1944, he joined the Mexican Agriculture Program (an initiative founded and funded by the Rockefeller Foundation) under which he produced about 6,000 new crosses over a decade, a huge quantity at a time when most breeders managed fewer than 200 per year. This quantity was essential to generating the high-performing outliers that could become popular new varieties. It is even more important when two traits you want (like yield and gluten content) are negatively correlated: The more varieties you test, the likelier you are to find one that bucks the trend, performing well on both.

Sources indicate that rather than approaching yield directly, the program focused on two main limiting factors: wheat rust and lodging. The intensive program of crossing and selecting made it possible to develop varieties that carried several forms of resistance to rust at once, and crossbreeding with Japanese “dwarf” wheat varieties, which were shorter and more robust, produced plants that could be juiced up with fertilizer without collapsing. By the 1960s, Borlaug had produced wheat varieties that had it all: resistance to lodging, multiple resistance to wheat rust, and high yields.

It has been revealed that one way this breeding program differed from previous ones was that it was split between two separate regions. The original purpose of this was to squeeze two growing seasons into one year, halving the time it took to produce a upcoming generation. After producing the first generation of offspring in the Toluca highlands, west of Mexico City, Borlaug moved the plants north to the lower-altitude Yaqui Valley, then produced the second generation in time to move back south for the following year. In these stages, selection was crude: Only varieties that failed to germinate or were affected by rust were culled. But later stages of the breeding program included yield trials and statistical selection methods.

According to recent reports, alternating between two regions had another, perhaps serendipitous, benefit.8 By advancing candidates that survived in both locations, Borlaug had selected those that could perform well across different environments. Selection for photoperiod-insensitive seeds (those able to mature in both despite differing daylight exposure) meant that varieties developed in Mexico might be successfully grown in other countries, and therefore could be shared across the world. Not all plants, and certainly not all wheat, can be photoperiod insensitive, but varieties tested by the Mexican Agriculture Program were, which may explain why wheat was the first crop to flourish in the Green Revolution. Maize, for example, is so sensitive that breeders operate semi-independent breeding programs for different latitudes.

If Ehrlich was aware of this work when he predicted mass starvation in 1968, he cannot have known its significance. In the mid-1960s, India and Pakistan began importing Borlaug’s new wheat varieties. One descendant of these imported wheats (called Kalyan Sona or “golden savior”) performed extremely well and became one of the most commonly planted varieties in the region. From 1965 to 1975, wheat yields in India and Pakistan nearly doubled;9 production increased so much and so swiftly that there were shortages of labor for harvest. Over time, other less developed countries followed a similar path.

The next stage of plant breeding was identifying specific genes for the precise properties that farmers wanted. The problem was that genotyping and genome sequencing were expensive and slow. The first genome was sequenced in 1977, but it belonged to a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) with a genome nearly a million times smaller than a human’s. Sequencing the first human genome cost somewhere between $300 million and $3 billion, and was achieved much later. And this was just a diploid human genome. Wheat has a genome five times larger than that, partly because of its three hybridized subgenomes.

Breeders came up with a comparatively quick and dirty solution: marker-assisted selection. Instead of tracking genes directly, they used much cruder tests to find genetic features (“markers”) that correlated with given traits. One technique was restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis, in which scientists use enzymes to chop DNA into pieces and then literally measure how long the resulting fragments are by how quickly they are pulled through gel by an electric current. While breeders would not know which genes were responsible for traits, they would know that a trait was correlated with a particular pattern of fragment lengths when cut with a particular enzyme.

Despite the crudeness of the method, it still worked for some traits, especially simple ones like rust resistance, which is often controlled by one or two genes. This allowed farmers and breeders to work out whether a variety was going to be good without going through a whole season of growing, as Norman Borlaug had to. This marker-assisted selection for many crops became routine in the 1990s. Field trials remained notable, but most strains were filtered out at the marker identification stage, and few ever made it to the field. At the beginning of the decade, only a few hundred markers were known, but by the end, this had expanded to thousands.

In a recent development, early marker-assisted selection was of limited use for traits like yield, which are influenced by thousands of genes. But we are no longer restricted to looking at a small number of genetic markers. DNA sequencing costs have decreased by a factor of 100,000 since 2000. Now breeders will often use “genomic selection”: essentially, using the entire genome as a marker and letting statistical software predict which genomes are associated with different traits. Genomic selection can tell us if 500 different genes each contribute 0.2% to a trait where traditional marker-assisted selection would have been useless.

In a recent development, this has revolutionized the process of plant breeding — if not the outcome.10 Global crop yields continue to increase at a steady rate, reflecting the fact that progress is getting harder to come by. We can now use the same genetic prediction tools for complex traits, like yield, grain quality, and drought tolerance, that we once did for simple ones. At the time Norman Borlaug was working, it took months or years and thousands of wheat plants to evaluate a new variety’s performance. Today, it can take just days to germinate a seedling and make predictions based on a small leaf sample.

Industry observers note that pessimists would say that wheat domesticated us, that we have spent thousands of years in backbreaking labor serving its reproductive ends. Optimists would argue our coevolution has benefited humanity far more, liberating us from a state of subsistence and creating a caloric surplus to sustain the lives of billions.

The human species used to live hand to mouth: Virtually all our labor was devoted to growing and harvesting food to fend off starvation. Now, in most developed countries, only a tiny fraction of the population works in agriculture. Wheat’s astonishing success is a crucial part of this change. It is the most widely grown crop on earth, covering 1.5% of the planet’s total land area, and is responsible for one-fifth of the world’s calorie intake. But the amount of labor required to produce those calories has decreased enormously. Since 1900, despite the world’s population increasing more than fourfold, the price of wheat is roughly a quarter of what it was.

In a recent development, that transformation is the result of sustained, incremental improvement to yield, to pathogen resistance, to ease of harvest, to taste, to gluten content, and much more. The advancements came from early farmers unknowingly favoring larger seeds; from finicky varieties that couldn’t handle frost, drought, and other hardships being killed off by the elements; and from breeders making active choices about what traits they wanted to cultivate, increasingly backed by the might of modern science. Today, we can sequence wheat’s entire genome and select for exactly the traits we want. Advances in breeding mean that similar stories can be told for every other major crop and farm animal. Each of us now enjoys the fruits of these advances at every mealtime.

It has been revealed that A lot has changed since the first wheat was farmed in the Fertile Crescent. But Enki is just as correct now as he was thousands of years ago: We would have no Sumer without grain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with a massive wave of mysteries and crime thrillers taking over movies, television, and even the world of podcasts, it was only a matter of time before somebody twisted the formula to make a lighter, more fun experience out of it. Only Murders in the Building did exactly that, and the Hulu series has unsurprisingly been on a real hot streak for the past half-decade. Going into its sixth season, Only Murders is still at the top of its game, delivering both mystery and comfort in equal measure.

Recent findings suggest that while Only Murders is probably the best of these lighter-hearted murder mysteries, it is far from the only one nowadays, and Netflix just added another that will likely share a lot of the same fan base. Mistletoe Murders, which is right now in its third season, shares a lot of the same energy as Only Murders in the Building, but the entire thing is gift-wrapped in holiday cheer.

Mistletoe Murders, for those who aren't familiar, is about a woman named Emily Lane who moves to a small town and opens a year-round Christmas store — just in time for a series of murders to strike the usually quiet town. The series stars Sarah Drew as Emily, while Peter Mooney stars as the mayor of Fletcher's Grove, Sam Wilner.

It's a simple premise, but it has understandably become a holiday season staple for many over the past three years. It began airing on Hallmark Channel back in 2024, and has released a new season each year as the holidays begin. Unlike the original movies on Hallmark that have to fit their stories into right, 82-minute windows each time, Mistletoe Murders has made great use of its format and allowed the mysteries themselves to simmer a lot more. It's the perfect blend of Hallmark's Christmas tone and the TV mysteries that air year-round.

While Mistletoe Murders is very much still an original to Hallmark Channel and Hallmark+, the organization struck a streaming deal to send previous seasons over the Netflix, likely hoping to get more attention on the show for its third season. Earlier this month, the first two seasons of Mistletoe Murders arrived on the Netflix lineup in the U.S. and have popped up on the streamer's Top 10 TV list since being added. So, in that regard, it appears Mistletoe Murders is already making plenty of new fans, making the move from Hallmark seem like an instant win.

The timing, of course, was no coincidence, as the third season of Mistletoe Murders just kicked off on November 5th. The night of Thanksgiving will see the fourth episode of Season 3 air on Hallmark, with two more episodes set to be released in December. The folks discovering the series are Netflix will be able to head over to Hallmark while Season 3 is still airing, and potentially remain fans for the inevitable Season 4 next year.
